newsitem.title: UK: BA plans 440 mln Ffr spend on Air Liberte.
newsitem.headline: BA plans 440 mln Ffr spend on Air Liberte.

text.p: British Airways said on Friday it has plans to spend 440 million francs ($84.5 million) on getting Air Liberte back into profit within three years if it takes over the insolvent French carrier.
Confirming French newspaper reports, a company spokesman said on Friday it has submitted the rescue plan to Liberte's administrator as part of its rescue bid.
"We would envisage investing about that sum (440 million francs) to restructure Air Liberte to enable it to return to profitability in about three years," he said.

The restructuring would involve dropping loss-making routes in addition to looking for ways of making the operation more efficient. "It would obviously be a gradual return to profitability," the spokesman said.

Analysts said this week that Air Liberte might go on losing money under BA for some time to come but that has been factored into the price BA is prepared to pay for it. BA has emphasised that its bid is only valid until the end of the month.

Air Liberte lost 650 million francs in the first nine months of 1996. But it controls about a quarter of all runway slots at Paris Orly airport and analysts said there is a belief that the air fare war which has plagued France's domestic market will have to end sooner or later.

They said Air France, which dominates the local market with its Air France Europe arm, cannot go on discounting fares because of the terms set by the European Commission for its state-subsidised rescue plan.
British Airways announced on Monday it had offered to buy Air Liberte for a nominal 25 million francs and plans eventually to merge Liberte with its existing local airline TAT.
French newspaper Les Echos quoted TAT chairman Marc Rochet on Firday as saying Air Liberte's situation was "catastrophic" and a turnaround would be difficult.
BA's bid prompted two French groups to bid for the carrier to create a French rival to Air France's domestic arm.
British entrepreneur Richard Branson's continental European carrier Virgin Express also said on Wednesday that it, too, might make a bid.
The French bidders are travel company Nouvelles Frontieres in a partnership with Royal Air Maroc and Banque Rivaud and a group led by AOM pilot Fernand Denan.

AOM is among the assets of state-owned Credit Lyonnais slated to be sold as part of a state bailout of the bank. AOM chairman Alexandre Courvelaire said in an interview with the Figaro Economie on Friday that he had wanted to buy Air Liberte's assets but was asked by the CDR state agency, which groups the Credit Lyonnais assets for sale, not to bid.
"It was their decision and one I regret," Courvelaire said. He said AOM's survival hinges on the creation of a domestic rival to Air France.
Nouvelles Frontieres chairman Jacques Maillot's business plan envisages the subsequent purchase of AOM and an eventual merger of AOM and Air Liberte.
Courvelaire said he proposed an alliance with Air Liberte in July but the deal fell through when Air Liberte's owners rejected a proposal for a 600 million franc capital increase.

After Air Liberte went into receivership, Courvelaire said he prepared a bid on AOM's behalf to acquire the bulk of Air Liberte's network. "It was designed to provide a credible French alternative to foreign offers," he said.

British Airways appealed to Brussels to block any bid by AOM for Air Liberte, saying that would constitute an illegal use of state aid. Courvelaire said his bid for Air Liberte's assets -- and not for the company -- would not have broken the rules.
Groupe Rivaud, which owns 32.3 percent of Air Liberte, would take 75-80 percent under the plan, according to French newspapers.
Le Monde previously reported that Prime Minister Alain Juppe was pushing for a domestic buyer for Air Liberte.
